blocks.text: Alongside the קקותא mentioned in the preceding article, two other forbidden birds are also named (Chulin 63a), the קיאי [p. 163] and the קקואי. Landau translates, without any justification: cormorant and pelican; apart from the fact that the pelican most probably bore a different name (cf. §. 227), it is also very strange that these two day-birds should be grouped with the owl. Buxdorf (Lex. p. 2107) more correctly takes the Talmudic names as designations of night birds, and perhaps the two kinds of owlet, the little owl and the pygmy owl, are meant here. קקואי, for which Aruch reads קיקאי, may, being related to Cheveche, be the larger owlet, and קואי, after dropping the reduplication, the smaller owlet*).
The Eared Owl.

The great eared owl is called ינשוף in Hebrew (Lev. 11, 17) and קפופא in Talmudic. Its eyes are directed forward, it screeches at night, and its face resembles that of the cat (Nidda 23a). On Berachoth 57b Raschi says: It has cheeks like a human being and is called צואיטא, Chouette, a name which, to be sure, is used for the short-eared owl.

Its appearance in a dream is an evil omen because of the ugliness of the bird and its partial resemblance to a human being (ibid.); yet Raschi's explanation of the word קפופא is highly uncertain. On Chulin 63a he translates it as Chouette, but also as Chauvesouri; on Berachoth ibid., quite correctly, solely as Chouette; whereas ibid. 58b, quite differently, as Vulture (bearded vulture, see §. 113).
The Middle Eared Owl.
Berachoth 57b states: The appearance of the bird קריא (or קריא) in a dream is an evil omen because of its ugliness.

The Targumim use the Talmudic word to translate the Hebrew כום (Lev. 11, 17), where Raschi explains it as ייב"ן, and in our Talmudic passage as ייבנ"ץ, Hibou. The French word designates the middle eared owl (the horned owl, also called the lesser eagle-owl).
The Sparrowhawk.

נץ (Chulin 42a and 63a). Raschi explains it both here and on Lev. 11, 16 as אישפריויר, Épervier, sparrowhawk. However, one manuscript of Raschi's commentary on that biblical passage has אושטוור, Astur, goshawk; the Tosephot (Chulin 63a. s.v. נץ) also maintain that נץ cannot mean sparrowhawk; and if we further note that Bochart (Hieroz. P. 2. lib. 2. c. 14, col. 245) translates נץ as Accipiter, the LXX as Ἱέραξ [hierax], Winer (R. Wb. s.v.) as goshawk, and likewise Rosenmüller (Bibl. Alterth. vol. 4, part 2, p. 304), then, since the Greek and Latin word designates the entire genus of small hard-winged birds of prey, namely those that have four bare toes, hooked talons and a curved beak, the so-called genus of the strikers, the word נץ too may be a more general name for goshawk, sparrowhawk and falcon, which would at the same time explain the variants in Raschi mentioned above. Only in one passage (Chulin 42a) does Raschi contrast the goshawk with the sparrowhawk, so that נץ means only sparrowhawk; this passage is treated in the following article.
The Goshawk.

Chulin 42a states: The נץ kills small fowl, the גם large fowl, which Raschi expands in explanation: The sparrowhawk kills sparrows and doves, whereas the גם, i.e. אוסטוייר (Italian Astore), goshawk, kills chickens and geese.
Aruch, however, reads גז for גם and explains it as owl, or falcon. Mussaphia refers to Jonathan, who translates עזניה in Lev. 11, 13 as בר גוא*); but עזניה is a kind of eagle, cf. §. 194.

The Selicha for the second of the 10 days of penitence (cited in the Tos. Chulin ibid. s.v. דריפת) likewise reads: מדרם גז ונץ; Jesaias Pick, however, reads in the latter passage: מדרם גם והגז and understands גז as the falcon and גם as the vulture, for which reason Fürstenthal, in his commentary on the Selichoth, reads וואטור (Vauture) for אוסטוייר in the above passage of Raschi; but the vulture has [p. 165] other designations in the Talmud, and the goshawk is rightly called גם (large) in contrast to the sparrowhawk, since it is twice the size of the latter. Cf. also Isserels on Jore Dea §. 57, 3 and on it Sifte Cohen lit. 16, who translates גם as falcon and goshawk.

Finally, it should be noted that Raschi's statements regarding the prey of the two birds are not quite correct, for the sparrowhawk kills only small birds such as finches and sparrows, whereas the goshawk for its part seizes doves and chickens; accordingly one would have to strike out in Raschi doves among the small fowl and geese among the large fowl. Cf., however, Midrasch Rabba (Schir ha-Schirim fol. 17, col. d).
The Noble Falcon.

Besides the name גם, by which some designate the falcon (see §. 191), this bird, which is also called gyrfalcon and hunting falcon, has yet other names. In Chulin 63a the בר חיריא (son of whiteness) is also included under למינהו (after its kind), the addition which the Bible has after נץ (§. 190). Who, asks the Talmud, is the בר חיריא? It is, comes the answer, the שורינקא (shrike). Here the noble falcon is meant. It is brown above with whitish spots, sometimes entirely white (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 270), hence that name בר חיריא. It is trained for hunting, the hunter sitting on horseback with the falcon beside him, which he releases at the sight of another bird (Sabbat 94a). Perhaps it is also called בואי, of which it is related that David once went out to catch the בואי (Sanhedrin 95a), see Aruch s.v. שכר; yet the word is explained by Raschi as a place name, by others as prey*).
The Eagle.
The eagle
נשר

is the king of birds (Chagigah 13b); its flight is swift and it does not tire easily (Aboth 5, 20), [p. 166] yet it fears the flycatcher (§. 259). Fabulous is the legend that it catches the young chamois, which are born on high mountains and could easily meet their death by falling down, and brings them back to their mother (B. batra 16b*).
